📝Comprehensive Study Notes & Mental ModelQuick Review
Expand NotesCollapse
Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 2-3 · **Prerequisites:** Tailwind justify-items utilities, Z-axis translation, Generated content from attributes, scale utilities, Tailwind UI Ecommerce kit, Tailwind theme variables, stroke The headline concept is `break-before-*`, the family of utilities that ask the browser to start the next page, column, or region on a fresh break right before an element. Everything else in this chapter is a Tailwind v4 reference roundup: `break-after-*` complements it, and a block of two-axis alignment shortcuts (`place-content-*`, `place-items-*`, `place-self-*`) replaces the verbose `justify-items-*` plus `align-items-*` boilerplate. A short note at the end covers `space-*` versus `gap` so you stop reaching for `space-y-4` on grids, then four framework installation guides (Gatsby, Laravel + Vite, Meteor, Ember.js), a note on layer-aware purge, the `@plugin` directive for legacy Tailwind v3 plugins, and the relationship-bound state variants (`group-*`, `peer-*`, `has-*`, `aria-*`, `data-*`).

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

A break (`break-before-*` / `break-after-*` / `break-inside-*`) is an instruction the layout engine obeys when it is splitting content across pages, columns, or regions. `columns-3` from chapter 024 turns an article into a three-column newspaper flow; `break-before-column` on the next `<h2>` forces that heading to start a new column. `place-content-*` and friends are vocabulary shortcuts: each one writes two CSS declarations, mirroring the relationship between `justify-content` and `align-content` on a container, or between `justify-self` and `align-self` on an item. Every entry in this chapter is a thin layer over an existing CSS declaration. The value is not new power, it is fewer characters to type and a consistent vocabulary across the team.

Key Code / CLI Example
<article className="columns-3 gap-8">
  <p>...</p>
  <h2 className="break-before-column text-xl font-semibold mt-6">Section A</h2>
  <p>...</p>
  <h2 className="break-before-column text-xl font-semibold mt-6">Section B</h2>
</article>
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

Direct DOM mutation or impure side effects during the render phase cause hydration mismatches, duplicate executions in Strict Mode, and stale closures. Always declare full dependency arrays in useEffect and never read state during render from outside the component tree.

📝Comprehensive Study Notes & Mental ModelQuick Review
Expand NotesCollapse
Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 1 · **Prerequisites:** Outline styles, Tailwind CSS: Utility-First Styling, Custom color tokens, Tailwind theme variables, CSS transition utilities, Break before an element The outline-styles chapter taught you that an outline is a line drawn *outside* the box, invisible to layout, and the safe surface for a keyboard focus ring. This chapter zooms in on the three utilities that decide how that line looks (`outline-<width>`, `outline-<color>`, `outline-offset-<n>`), the `ring-*` alternative built from box-shadow, the `scale-*` transform, the `underline` / `line-through` text-decoration family, and the four transition utilities that animate all of it: `transition-<group>`, `duration-<n>`, `delay-<n>`, and `ease-*`. Every one of these is difficulty 1. The value is in the combinations: a focus ring that fades in over 200ms, a card that scales up on hover, a "done" item that strikes through with a coloured line.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Outline width, colour, and offset are the accessibility surface: a focus ring that a keyboard user can see, that high-contrast mode can force to a system colour, and that never shifts layout when it appears. The ring utilities give you the same indicator when you want it to hug rounded corners. Scale is the hover/press affordance on every interactive card and button in a modern UI. Text-decoration lines carry meaning (a struck-through price, a completed task) that colour alone should not carry. And the four transition families are what separate a UI that snaps harshly from one that feels considered, all without a single line of JavaScript animation code. You will apply these together on nearly every button, link, and card you build for the rest of the course.

Key Code / CLI Example
<button className="outline-2 outline-sky-500 outline-offset-2">Save</button>
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

1. **`outline-2` with no colour on a light background.** The width is set, but `outline-color` defaults to the element's `currentColor` (its text colour). On a white button with dark text you get a dark ring you did not design. Always pair a width with an explicit `outline-<color>` (or `ring-<color>`). 2. **Expecting `outline-offset` to animate the box.** It animates the *gap*, not the box size, which is exactly why it is safe. If you meant to grow the element, that is `scale-*` or a size utility, not offset. 3. **Reaching for `transition-all` by default.** It animates every property, including layout properties like `height` and `width` that reflow. A hover that changes `height` under `transition-all` will visibly lurch. Use the narrowest group: `transition-colors`, `transition-transform`

📝Comprehensive Study Notes & Mental ModelQuick Review
Expand NotesCollapse
Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 1-3 · **Prerequisites:** CSS transition utilities, Break before an element, Outline styles, Outline width, Background color, image, size, and position utilities, Tailwind theme variables, stroke This chapter is the wider Tailwind vocabulary that surrounds `transition-*` and the transform families. It collects the property-list extensions, the accessibility-aware variants, the interactivity utilities, the motion-preference variants, and the few transform-adjacent families that did not fit in the CSS transition utilities chapter. Each section is short on prose and dense on tables.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

A Tailwind UI is a contract with the user as much as it is a set of classes. Each interactive utility answers a question: *what animates*, *who gets it*, *when does it fire*, *does the user know it's moving*. The contracts layer on top of each other: Read the class string once per layer. The first layer says what animates. The second layer says which user states it applies to. The third layer says how it degrades for users who opted out.

Key Code / CLI Example
@import "tailwindcss";

@theme {
  --card-properties: width, height, color, background-color, box-shadow;
}
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

// right: branch between complete strings. className={kind === "color" ? "transition-colors" : "transition-transform"} ``` The full class name is never a literal in a scanned file, so the scanner does not generate CSS for it. The style silently does nothing. Branch between complete strings or build a `Record<Kind, string>` of complete class strings. A user who has asked the OS for less motion still sees the lift. The WCAG-recommended fix is to pair every animated utility with `motion-reduce:`: Forgetting the `motion-reduce:` on a *single* utility breaks the user's accessibility setting without warning. Audit class strings for any `transition-*`, `duration-*`, `delay-*`, `animate-*`, `scale-*`, `rotate-*`, or `translate-*`; each is a candidate.

Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 1-3 · **Prerequisites:** Transition property utilities, Tailwind theme variables, stroke, Z-axis translation, Width and height utilities, Break before an element, overscroll-behavior utilities, Custom color tokens, Tailwind CSS: Utility-First Styling, Tailwind UI Ecommerce kit, Generated content from attributes This is a reference-heavy Tailwind chapter. Its main subject is `perspective-origin`, with a compact reference roundup for related Tailwind v4 configuration and interaction utilities used in the exercises.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Imagine a small card floating in front of a camera. `perspective-*` chooses how close the camera is. `perspective-origin-*` moves the camera's vanishing point across the card. The card can use the same `rotate-y-12` transform in both cases, yet the tilt appears to lean toward a different corner. The origin is a coordinate on the element being projected. It does not move the element by itself. A 3D transform must be present before changing the origin can produce a visible difference.

Key Code / CLI Example
export function OriginPreview() {
  return (
    <div className="grid grid-cols-2 gap-6">
      <div className="perspective-near">
        <div className="perspective-origin-top-left transform-3d rotate-y-12 rounded-lg bg-sky-500 p-6 text-white">
          top left
        </div>
      </div>
      <div className="perspective-near">
        <div className="perspective-origin-bottom-right transform-3d rotate-y-12 rounded-lg bg-indigo-500 p-6 text-white">
          bottom right
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

This deliberately broken TypeScript does not compile: function Origin({ value }: { value: string }) { const className: string = origins[value as keyof typeof origins]; return <div className={className} />; } ``` A stricter and safer version accepts the union at the component boundary: function Origin({ value }: { value: Origin }) { return <div className={origins[value]} />; } ```

Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 1-3 · **Prerequisites:** Custom color tokens, perspective-origin, Outline styles, Break before an element, stroke Effects are the surface layer of a UI. They make cards lift, text punch through a busy hero, and a frosted modal read like glass instead of cardboard. Tailwind groups all of these under one roof, calling them *effects*. Most are zero-runtime utility wrappers around a CSS property: `shadow-*` wraps `box-shadow`, `opacity-*` wraps `opacity`, `mix-blend-*` wraps `mix-blend-mode`, `mask-*` wraps the mask family, and `backdrop-*` wraps the backdrop-filter family.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Every modern UI pulls from this toolkit: a hero headline drops a text shadow, a card lifts on hover, a modal blurs its backdrop, a price tag multiplies into the card. Treating the effect utilities as a vocabulary (a `box-shadow` story, a `text-shadow` story, an `opacity` story, a `filter` story, a `mix-blend-mode` story, a `mask` story, a `prose` story) keeps every component pulled from the same palette. The classes live in the same `className` strings as the layout utilities from earlier chapters, so a fully styled component is one string per element.

Key Code / CLI Example
<button
  type="button"
  className="rounded-md bg-white px-4 py-2 text-slate-900
             shadow-md hover:shadow-lg
             focus-visible:outline-none focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-sky-500
             dark:bg-slate-800 dark:text-slate-100"
>
  Save
</button>
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

Tailwind's scanner does not see the assembled string, so the utility is missing from the generated CSS. The element renders with no shadow at all, and the bug surfaces only in production builds where unused utilities are stripped. Map values to complete strings instead. `opacity` is multiplied across every rendered pixel of the element and its children. The title and the body fade with the surface. If the goal is a translucent surface with crisp text, reach for `bg-sky-500/30` instead and leave `text-*` fully opaque. Without an isolating ancestor, `mix-blend-mode` composites against everything behind the element in the stacking context, including the page background. The multiply can produce unexpected colours when the layout shifts. Wrap the card in `isolate` (or any `position: relative

📝Comprehensive Study Notes & Mental ModelQuick Review
Expand NotesCollapse
Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 1-2 · **Prerequisites:** Shadows, opacity, blending, and isolation CSS `filter` accepts a chain of effects: `contrast(150%) grayscale(50%) hue-rotate(45deg)`. Tailwind splits the chain into single-purpose utilities that compose on the element. `backdrop-filter` is the same idea applied to whatever is behind the element, which is only visible when the element itself is translucent. `drop-shadow` is the filter-family version of `box-shadow`, and it follows the rendered silhouette instead of the box.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Filters show up the moment a UI stops being a stack of rectangles: a hero photo that needs more punch, a logo that needs to flip in dark mode, a frosted modal scrim, a coloured drop-shadow on an SVG icon. Tailwind's filter families are the canonical place to reach for them; CSS exposes the same primitives, but the utility form lets you keep all of styling in `className` so the design tokens and the component logic live in the same file. - `filter-*` on the element, `backdrop-*` on what is behind. They compose independently. - `drop-shadow-*` follows the silhouette; `shadow-*` follows the box. For SVG, PNG-with-transparency, or text, `drop-shadow` is correct; for cards, modals, and other rectangles, `shadow` is correct.

Key Code / CLI Example
<img className="contrast-50 ..." src="/photo.jpg" alt="Low contrast" />
<img className="contrast-100 ..." src="/photo.jpg" alt="Identity" />
<img className="contrast-150 hover:contrast-200 ..." src="/photo.jpg" alt="Boosted" />
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

`drop-shadow-lg` on a rectangular div produces the same result as `shadow-lg`. The cost is higher: `drop-shadow` runs through the silhouette pass even though the silhouette is the same as the box. For rectangles, `shadow-lg` is the right tool. Reach for `drop-shadow` only when the silhouette is non-rectangular: SVG icons, PNG logos with transparency, text glyphs. `bg-white` is opaque; the backdrop blur has nothing to blur. The element looks like a plain white card. Pair every `backdrop-*` utility with a `/<opacity>` colour modifier (`bg-white/30`, `bg-slate-900/40`). These are two different effects. `saturate-150` recolours the image pixels. `backdrop-saturate-150` recolours the pixels behind the `bg-slate-900` element. They look similar in a screenshot, but the underlying filter declara

📝Comprehensive Study Notes & Mental ModelQuick Review
Expand NotesCollapse
Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 2-3 · **Prerequisites:** Perspective origin, Tailwind theme variables, Custom color tokens, Tailwind UI Ecommerce kit, Tailwind CSS Just-In-Time engine, Static asset URL import Tailwind generates one CSS file that contains every utility your content scan touched. Two utilities that target the same property (`bg-blue-500` and `bg-red-500`) end up as two rules with the same specificity. The browser applies whichever rule appears later in the source order; the order of class names on the element is irrelevant. The same applies when Tailwind sits next to legacy CSS that uses IDs or `!important`: Tailwind's specificity is class-only, so legacy rules win unless Tailwind is forced to be `!important` globally.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

The cascade is the part of Tailwind most projects get wrong without knowing it. A designer asks "why does this button not turn blue on hover?", a developer reorders class names, nothing happens, the developer adds `!important` to the rule that should lose, the page becomes unmaintainable. None of those fixes address the actual cause: class-name order is not the cascade. The features in this chapter (the `!` modifier, the global `important` mode, the `@apply` directive, the `--alpha()` function, the `@layer` ordering, the `peer-*` and `group-*` variants, the `type:` hint) are the tools that make the cascade do what you want without `!important` on every rule. The version notes are a paper trail: if you inherit a v3 project and need to know whether `flex-shrink` or `shrink` is the right class, the v4 changelog is the answer.

Key Code / CLI Example
<button className="bg-red-500 hover:bg-blue-500">Save</button>
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

The two are equivalent. The class attribute is not a stylesheet; the browser applies both rules, and the one that appears later in the *generated* CSS wins. Reordering class names to "make the override win" is a no-op. The `!` makes the red `!important`. The hover fires, the blue wins because the blue rule is the only one matching the hover state, and the red rule (even though important) does not match the hover state. The button is blue on hover. The `!` is not a "make this state win", it is a "make this declaration unkillable by non-important rules". Without `@layer components` (or any `@layer`), the rule sits in the author's layer, which is the lowest specificity in the cascade. A `<button className="bg-red-500">` inside the rule would lose, even though utilities are supposed to overr

2 Lessons 00m00s / 00m00s

06m20s

In-depth walkthrough of Tailwind v4 default style changes, examining real-world production implementations, rendering performance, and TypeScript contracts.

Official Documentation References
Tailwind CSS Official Documentation — Utility-first CSS framework for rapid UI development.
Tailwind CSS: Responsive Design — Mobile-first breakpoint modifiers (sm, md, lg, xl, 2xl).
📝Comprehensive Study Notes & Mental ModelQuick Review
Expand NotesCollapse
Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 3 · **Prerequisites:** Global important mode and utility conflicts, perspective-origin, CSS transition utilities, Outline width, Break before an element, Transition property utilities, Background color, image, size, and position utilities, Tailwind CSS: Utility-First Styling, Currying event-handler factories, Tailwind theme variables, Custom color tokens, stroke Tailwind v4 is a rewrite, not a rename. The utility names you already know mostly survived, so a `bg-rose-500` from a v3 codebase still works in v4. What changed is the ground under those names: the Preflight defaults, the CSS properties the transform utilities emit, the order stacked variants apply, and the syntax for arbitrary values. A migration is mostly an audit: walk every place you relied on a v3 default and decide whether the new default is what you want or whether you have to restate it.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Tailwind v4 keeps the utility names that made Tailwind popular and rebuilds the engine underneath. The className strings you write are mostly unchanged; the CSS those strings compile to has shifted in ways that affect borders, rings, placeholders, buttons, dialogs, transforms, and the variant order. A migration that does not audit these defaults ships subtle visual regressions: a border that paints in `currentColor` instead of gray-200, a focus ring that is 1px instead of 3px, a placeholder that is solid instead of 60% opacity, a button cursor that is `default` instead of `pointer`. You will meet this in real codebases in three places. First, a v3 project you inherit gets the v4 upgrade and the audit checklist is your first task. Second, a v4 design system you build has to choose whether to accept the new defaults or restate the old ones; the `@theme` block is the right place to set the project-wide preferences. Third, a v4 dependency you consume (a UI kit, a design-system package) may rely on `@theme inline` or `theme(static)`, and you have to know the difference to debug "why is my variable empty in production?" bugs.

Key Code / CLI Example
/* v4 output */
.border { border-color: currentColor; }
.border-2 { border-color: currentColor; border-width: 2px; }
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

In v4 it paints `currentColor`. A card with `className="border p-4"` whose parent is dark-mode-on will have a white border on a dark background. If you wanted gray-200 (the v3 default), write `border-gray-200`. v4 ignores `bg-opacity-50`. Replace with `bg-red-500/50`. v4 renamed them. `shrink-0` and `grow-1` are the v4 spellings. A v3 codebase migrating to v4 needs every `flex-shrink-*` and `flex-grow-*` swapped. `overflow-ellipsis` is removed; `text-ellipsis` is the v4 spelling. A global find-and-replace handles most migrations.

Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 3 · **Prerequisites:** Global important mode and utility conflicts, perspective-origin, CSS transition utilities, Outline width, Break before an element, Transition property utilities, Background color, image, size, and position utilities, Tailwind CSS: Utility-First Styling, Currying event-handler factories, Tailwind theme variables, Custom color tokens, stroke Tailwind v4 is a rewrite, not a rename. The utility names you already know mostly survived, so a `bg-rose-500` from a v3 codebase still works in v4. What changed is the ground under those names: the Preflight defaults, the CSS properties the transform utilities emit, the order stacked variants apply, and the syntax for arbitrary values. A migration is mostly an audit: walk every place you relied on a v3 default and decide whether the new default is what you want or whether you have to restate it.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Tailwind v4 keeps the utility names that made Tailwind popular and rebuilds the engine underneath. The className strings you write are mostly unchanged; the CSS those strings compile to has shifted in ways that affect borders, rings, placeholders, buttons, dialogs, transforms, and the variant order. A migration that does not audit these defaults ships subtle visual regressions: a border that paints in `currentColor` instead of gray-200, a focus ring that is 1px instead of 3px, a placeholder that is solid instead of 60% opacity, a button cursor that is `default` instead of `pointer`. Second, a v4 design system you build has to choose whether to accept the new defaults or restate the old ones; the `@theme` block is the right place to set the project-wide preferences. Third, a v4 dependency you consume (a UI kit, a design-system package) may rely on `@theme inline` or `theme(static)`, and you have to know the difference to debug "why is my variable empty in production?" bugs.

⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

If you wanted gray-200 (the v3 default), write `border-gray-200`. v4 ignores `bg-opacity-50`. Replace with `bg-red-500/50`. v4 renamed them. `shrink-0` and `grow-1` are the v4 spellings. A v3 codebase migrating to v4 needs every `flex-shrink-*` and `flex-grow-*` swapped. `overflow-ellipsis` is removed; `text-ellipsis` is the v4 spelling. Core Definition & Architectural Role

A component library is like a box of tested building parts. You assemble buttons, alerts, navigation, and forms instead of cutting every piece from raw CSS. The tradeoff is that the parts arrive with an API and a visual opinion.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Component libraries shorten routine UI work and make interaction patterns consistent. Their props also become architectural boundaries: application state enters through typed props, events leave through callbacks, and theme values coordinate the screen. Knowing where the library stops prevents accessibility regressions, invalid prop values, and state hidden inside visual components.

Key Code / CLI Example
bun add @mui/material @emotion/react @emotion/styled
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

Installing only `@mui/material` can produce: Install `@emotion/react` and `@emotion/styled` with MUI's core package. This is deliberately broken: Use `variant="contained"`, or augment MUI's variant types when your theme defines a real custom variant.

Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 1 · **Prerequisites:** Component Libraries: Material UI This chapter is a reference roundup. The page covers the `Chip` family in depth (the slug's namesake), then summarises a dozen neighbouring Material UI primitives: `List`, `ImageList`, `ButtonGroup`, `Alert`, `Avatar`, `Backdrop`, `Badge`, `Button`, `Card`, `Checkbox`, and `Container`. Each entry is what the component is for, its signature props, and one minimal JSX. The two exercises at the end pull several of them into one UI slice and then re-type the slice with strict TypeScript.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

A `Chip` is the small, rounded pill that lives in three places: filters at the top of a list view, tags on a content card, and inline status messages next to a user avatar. It is the smallest interactive thing Material UI ships, and it borrows from three of the bigger components: - `Avatar` for the leading ornament (`avatar` prop), - `Icon` for the leading or trailing glyph (`icon` prop, or the delete-icon from `onDelete`), - `ButtonBase` for the underlying click affordance (when `onClick` or `onDelete` is set, the chip is a button in the tab order).

Key Code / CLI Example
bun add @mui/material @emotion/react @emotion/styled
bun add @mui/icons-material
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

Direct DOM mutation or impure side effects during the render phase cause hydration mismatches, duplicate executions in Strict Mode, and stale closures. Always declare full dependency arrays in useEffect and never read state during render from outside the component tree.

Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 1 · **Prerequisites:** Chip, Component Libraries: Material UI This chapter covers two things. First, the deep-import rule that keeps Material UI's dev server fast (barrel imports do not change the production bundle, but they do slow startup and rebuild). Second, a reference roundup of nine neighbouring MUI primitives you will reach for next to `Chip` and `Button`: `Divider`, `Fab`, `Link`, `Paper`, `Progress` indicators, `RadioGroup`, `Skeleton`, the `createTheme` / `ThemeProvider` pair, and the responsive viewport meta tag. The two exercises at the end combine most of these into one UI slice and then re-type it under strict TypeScript.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Material UI's package layout is a directory of files with one default export per file, plus one barrel file (`index.js`) that re-exports them all. Your bundler can resolve either path: In production, both paths ship the same tree-shaken result. In development, the barrel forces the dev server to parse every named export to learn which symbols exist before it can throw a `ReferenceError` when you mistype one. That parse takes a long time. The `@mui/icons-material` package is worse: it ships 2,100+ components, and the barrel parse takes long enough that you can watch it happen.

Key Code / CLI Example
import Button from '@mui/material/Button';
import DeleteIcon from '@mui/icons-material/Delete';

export default function ConfirmDelete() {
  return (
    <Button
      variant="contained"
      color="error"
      startIcon={<DeleteIcon />}
      onClick={() => console.log('confirmed')}
    >
      Delete account
    </Button>
  );
}
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

ESLint with the `no-restricted-imports` pattern from above reports: Replace with `import Button from '@mui/material/Button';`. Add `@mui/icons-material/[IconName]` for icons. VS Code by default adds barrel-import suggestions. Stop that for MUI with a project-scoped setting: `@mui/icons-material` depends on `@mui/material`, which depends on Emotion. Installing the icon package without the core produces runtime errors when the first icon mounts:

Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 1 · **Prerequisites:** Chip, Component Libraries: Material UI This chapter is a reference roundup. The slug's namesake, **MUI Supported Components**, frames Material UI's scope: the library ships the practical building blocks of Material Design but does not promise every component or every guideline feature. Around that, the page documents **Supported Platforms** (which browsers, runtimes, and bundlers are first-class), the **System props to `sx`** codemod for the v6/v9 migration, the **TextareaAutosize** utility that auto-grows a `<textarea>`, the **Timeline** lab component for chronological content, the **Versioning Strategy** (semantic versioning with deprecation windows), the **Changelog Policy** (`CHANGELOG.md` for the current major, `CHANGELOG.old.md` for archives), the **Long-Term Support** policy (security and regression fixes for the predecessor major), and the four core building blocks the rest of the section leans on: **Paper** (surface + elevation), **Card** (paper with composable parts), **Alert** (transient feedback with severity), **Progress** (LinearProgress and CircularProgress), and **Radio** + **RadioGroup** (roving-tabindex single-select).

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Material UI's stance is explicit: it provides the practical building blocks developers need to build compelling user interfaces, omitting incidental or rarely-used components. The library does not aim to implement every Material Design component or every guideline feature. If a component exists in the Material Design specification but has no clear use in real apps, it does not ship in `@mui/material`. If you need it, you either build it yourself or reach for a community extension in `@mui/x` or a related project. The practical effect of this scope:

Key Code / CLI Example
bun add @mui/material @emotion/react @emotion/styled

Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 1 · **Prerequisites:** Chip, Component Libraries: Material UI This chapter is a reference roundup. The slug's namesake, **MUI Supported Components**, frames Material UI's scope: the library ships the practical building blocks of Material Design but does not promise every component or every guideline feature. Around that, the page documents **Supported Platforms** (which browsers, runtimes, and bundlers are first-class), the **System props to `sx`** codemod for the v6/v9 migration, the **TextareaAutosize** utility that auto-grows a `<textarea>`, the **Timeline** lab component for chronological content, the **Versioning Strategy** (semantic versioning with deprecation windows), the **Changelog Policy** (`CHANGELOG.md` for the current major, `CHANGELOG.old.md` for archives), the **Long-Term Support** policy (security and regression fixes for the predecessor major), and the four core building blocks the rest of the section leans on: **Paper** (surface + elevation), **Card** (paper with composable parts), **Alert** (transient feedback with severity), **Progress** (LinearProgress and CircularProgress), and **Radio** + **RadioGroup** (roving-tabindex single-select).

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Material UI's stance is explicit: it provides the practical building blocks developers need to build compelling user interfaces, omitting incidental or rarely-used components. The library does not aim to implement every Material Design component or every guideline feature. If a component exists in the Material Design specification but has no clear use in real apps, it does not ship in `@mui/material`. If you need it, you either build it yourself or reach for a community extension in `@mui/x` or a related project. The practical effect of this scope:

Key Code / CLI Example
bun add @mui/material @emotion/react @emotion/styled
bun add @mui/icons-material
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

Direct DOM mutation or impure side effects during the render phase cause hydration mismatches, duplicate executions in Strict Mode, and stale closures. Always declare full dependency arrays in useEffect and never read state during render from outside the component tree.

Core Definition & Architectural Role

A hardware shop sorts parts by job: switches control power, gauges display values, and fasteners join pieces. Material UI's catalog works the same way. Start with the job your interface must perform, then choose a component from the matching category. **Difficulty:** 1 · **Prerequisites:** Pagination Query Parameters, Component Libraries: Material UI, Chip

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Real screens mix categories. A settings page may use `TextField`, `Select`, `Switch`, `Divider`, `Button`, and `Snackbar` in one component tree. Choosing by behavior prevents controls that look right but carry the wrong semantics. Controlled props keep application state visible, theme context keeps visual decisions consistent, and matching skeleton dimensions prevents layout shifts while data loads.

Key Code / CLI Example
import Button from '@mui/material/Button';
import Chip from '@mui/material/Chip';
import Divider from '@mui/material/Divider';
import Stack from '@mui/material/Stack';

export default function Actions() {
  return (
    <Stack spacing={2} divider={<Divider flexItem />}>
      <Chip label="Draft" size="small" />
      <Button variant="contained">Publish</Button>
    </Stack>
  );
}
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

This is deliberately broken: Use `variant="contained"`, or add a typed theme variant before using a custom name. A visual placeholder is not a label. An unlabeled `Select` may produce an accessibility audit such as: Connect `InputLabel` and `Select` with `labelId`, or use `TextField` with `select` and `label`.

Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 1-2 · **Prerequisites:** Material UI component catalog, Material UI deep imports for bundle size, Component Libraries: Material UI, Chip, Conditional Rendering and Lists This chapter is a reference roundup. The headline topic is Material UI's color architecture (palettes, shades, and the `theme.spacing` scale), but the page also covers the supporting surfaces and patterns you reach for when you wire a theme into a real app: `CssBaseline` for normalization, `Paper` for elevation, `Skeleton` for loading placeholders, the `default-theme` viewer for inspection, the Figma design kit for designer-developer parity, locale text, the `theme.zIndex` scale, the `slots` / `slotProps` / `component` composition contract, the boolean-versus-enum prop convention, the tree-shaking rule, and the experimental API stability contract.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

A Material UI color object is a colour dictionary in the same shape as Material Design's design tokens. Each colour has a `main` shade, a `light` and `dark` companion, and a `contrastText` shade that picks readable text on top of `main`. The palette tokens you address in components (`primary`, `secondary`, `error`, `warning`, `info`, `success`) are slots on a `palette` object that each reference a colour object. You can either hand-build a color object (good for full control) or import a prebuilt hue from `@mui/material/colors` and pass its `main` shade into `createTheme` (good for a quick branded seed). Components read the `palette.primary.main` token through React context, so the same colour shows up everywhere without prop drilling.

Key Code / CLI Example
bun add @mui/material @emotion/react @emotion/styled
bun add @mui/icons-material
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

The locale is not a `ThemeProvider` prop. The compiler does not always catch this because both accept a string-shaped prop. Pass the locale to `createTheme`: If a `Snackbar` or `Tooltip` mounts at the same time, your backdrop sits behind them. Read `theme.zIndex.drawer + 1` (or whichever neighbour you need to be above) and let the theme own the layering scale. The import works. The next minor release can rename or remove it. Add a comment at the call site so the next maintainer knows the surface is unstable and can plan a migration. `component` swaps the root element; the `variant` styles then target a `<div>` instead of a `<button>`. The result looks the same visually but loses the button semantics (no form submission, no native click activation). Use `component` for router links and s

Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 2 · **Prerequisites:** Component Libraries: Material UI, Chip, Material UI component catalog, Material UI Color System This chapter is a reference roundup. The slug's namesake, **Keyboard navigation and focus**, frames how Material UI implements WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices out of the box: tabs move with arrow keys, dialogs trap focus inside the modal and restore it on close, menus support type-ahead, and `Tooltip` wraps disabled children in a `<span>` so they can receive focus. Around that, the page documents the neighbouring MUI primitives and APIs that this chapter covers: **Accordion** (a collapsible region with `AccordionSummary` / `AccordionDetails`), **AppBar** (top-of-page chrome), **BottomNavigation** (the mobile top-level dest switcher), the **Breakpoints** API (`up` / `down` / `only` / `between`), **ClickAwayListener** (close-on-outside-click utility), **CSS Theme Variables** (token-based theming via custom properties), the **Customization Strategy Ladder** (sx -> styled -> theme overrides -> global CSS), the **Figma design kit** vocabulary, the **Grid v1 -> Grid v2** migration, the **Icon APIs** (packaged SVG, custom `SvgIcon`, fonts through `Icon`), **ImageList** (the modernised grid list), **MUI Lab** (the `@mui/lab` incubator package), **List** (the semantic list primitive), and **Masonry** (variable-height columns).

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Keyboard navigation and focus is a contract between every interactive MUI primitive and the user agent: the component owns the keyboard behaviour, the ARIA roles, and the focus management. You write JSX with `value`, `onChange`, and content; MUI ships the arrow-key roving tabindex on `Tabs`, the focus trap on `Dialog`, and the type-ahead buffer on `Autocomplete`. The job you do as a developer is to make sure the props you pass carry an accessible name and the layout you build does not break the focus order. Each primitive in the roundup below carries its own keyboard contract; the rest of the chapter is reference material grouped around that idea, the same way Material UI component catalog groups primitives by interface job.

Key Code / CLI Example
bun add @mui/material @emotion/react @emotion/styled
bun add @mui/icons-material
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

Direct DOM mutation or impure side effects during the render phase cause hydration mismatches, duplicate executions in Strict Mode, and stale closures. Always declare full dependency arrays in useEffect and never read state during render from outside the component tree.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that connects an AI client to trusted sources of documentation and code. The Material UI MCP server is a small package that runs on your machine and speaks to the client over the `stdio` transport. When the client asks a question about MUI, the server returns passages from the official docs and code from the published component registries, so the answer quotes a real page and links to a URL that resolves. You add it to a client with one command. In Claude Code:

Key Code / CLI Example
claude mcp add mui-mcp -- npx -y @mui/mcp@latest

Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 2 · **Prerequisites:** Material UI component catalog, Material UI Color System, Component Libraries: Material UI, Chip, Material UI deep imports for bundle size, Material UI MCP documentation server This chapter is a reference roundup. The headline topic is the `ThemeProvider` and the `createTheme` factory, but the page also covers the surfaces and patterns you reach for when you wire a theme into a real app: scoping MUI alongside another styling system with `THEME_ID`, the `theme.transitions.create` and `getAutoHeightDuration` motion helpers, the theme's `components` section for default-props and slot-level overrides, the `TransferList` shuttle composition pattern, the five transition primitives (`Collapse`, `Fade`, `Grow`, `Slide`, `Zoom`), the migration paths from v0 to v1 and v3 to v4, the v5 component-level and style-level breaking changes, the v7 `enableCssLayer` and standardized slots update, the `theme.zIndex` scale, the minimal-bug-reproduction rule for filing MUI issues, the bundle-size minimization story, and the `Modal` primitive that `Dialog`, `Drawer`, `Menu`, and `Popover` all build on.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

The `ThemeProvider` is a React context provider whose value is a fully built `Theme` object. `createTheme(options)` walks the options, fills every unset token from a default, and returns a complete, deeply-typed `Theme`. The provider hands that theme down the tree, and every MUI component (and every `styled` / `sx` / `useTheme` call) reads it from context. Move the provider, change the theme; the visible app re-themes without a single prop-drilled colour. When two styling systems coexist in the same tree (MUI plus Theme UI, MUI plus Chakra, MUI plus a custom design-token context), the providers must agree on which context key carries which theme. MUI exposes `THEME_ID` for exactly that negotiation: a string constant you put on a non-default context, so MUI's `styled`, `sx`, and `useTheme` look up the right value while other libraries keep using the default key.

Key Code / CLI Example
bun add @mui/material @emotion/react @emotion/styled
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

`useTheme` from `@mui/material/styles` looks up the value under the `THEME_ID` constant, not under `myCustomKey`. The button will render with the default theme or throw depending on the MUI version. Use `[THEME_ID]: materialTheme`. The property is `theme.transitions.duration.standard`. `theme.duration` is undefined. A rename of the namespace would be a breaking change, so the chain stays as is. The button's icon slot is `startIcon` and `endIcon`, not `icon`. The wrong name compiles because the slot map is open-ended, but the override never applies. The fix is the slot name printed in the component's `slots` table. A `Snackbar` at `zIndex.tooltip` or a `Dialog` at `zIndex.modal` can stack above the hand-picked number. Use `theme.zIndex.drawer + 1` (or whichever neighbour the backdrop nee

MUI exposes `THEME_ID` for exactly that negotiation: a string constant you put on a non-default context, so MUI's `styled`, `sx`, and `useTheme` look up the right value while other libraries keep using the default key.

Key Code / CLI Example
bun add @mui/material @emotion/react @emotion/styled
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

`useTheme` from `@mui/material/styles` looks up the value under the `THEME_ID` constant, not under `myCustomKey`. The button will render with the default theme or throw depending on the MUI version. Use `[THEME_ID]: materialTheme`. The property is `theme.transitions.duration.standard`. `theme.duration` is undefined. A rename of the namespace would be a breaking change, so the chain stays as is. The button's icon slot is `startIcon` and `endIcon`, not `icon`. The wrong name compiles because the slot map is open-ended, but the override never applies. The fix is the slot name printed in the component's `slots` table. A `Snackbar` at `zIndex.tooltip` or a `Dialog` at `zIndex.modal` can stack above the hand-picked number. Use `theme.zIndex.drawer + 1` (or whichever neighbour the backdrop nee

**Difficulty:** 2 · **Prerequisites:** Material UI theme provider, Component Libraries: Material UI, Material UI component catalog This chapter is a reference roundup. The headline topic is the `Dialog` family and the small constellation of surfaces that share MUI's `Modal` primitive, but the page also covers the panels that flank a screen (`Drawer`, `SwipeableDrawer`, `Popover`), the scroll lock behind every modal, the disclosure and message components that sit alongside a dialog (`Accordion`, `Alert`), the top-of-screen surface (`AppBar`, `Toolbar`), and the responsive helpers (`breakpoints`, `useMediaQuery`, `Grid`, theme `Typography`, MUI's API design rules) that switch a dialog between desktop and full-screen mobile.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

A `Dialog` is a paper panel that floats above the page, traps focus, and blocks the rest of the screen until dismissed. Under the hood it is `Dialog` content composed inside `Modal`. The same `Modal` primitive powers `Drawer`, `Popover`, `Menu`, and the dropdown half of `Select`. Reach for one of those higher-level components whenever the surface matches its job; reach for `Modal` directly only when you need a custom positioner (a video lightbox, a centered tooltip). The `Modal` primitive is the seam: backdrop, focus trap, scroll lock, portal. Every higher-level surface inherits those behaviours and adds one more concern (a paper panel for `Dialog`, an anchor position for `Drawer`/`Popover`, an item list for `Menu`).

const theme: Theme = createTheme({
  palette: { primary: { main: '#0052cc' } },
  shape: { borderRadius: 8 },
});

export function App(): JSX.Element {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
  return (
    <ThemeProvider theme={theme}>
      <Button variant="contained" color="primary" onClick={() => setOpen(true)}>
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

A screen reader announces a dialog with no name (failures of the same kind as a button without an accessible name). Pair the title's `id` with the dialog's `aria-labelledby`: Mobile and desktop want different drawer behaviour. The wrong answer is to render `<Drawer variant="temporary">` everywhere and toggle `open` everywhere; the user on desktop still has to click the menu icon to see the sidebar. The right answer is the responsive swap with `useMediaQuery`. Without `open` and `onClose`, the popover never renders. Both props are required for a controlled popover. Same `open` / `onClose` pair as `Dialog` and `Drawer`. When a `Dialog` opens, the body scrollbar disappears. The banner, which ignores the scrollbar, visibly shifts left. Add the `mui-fixed` class to the banner root and MUI co

**Difficulty:** 2 · **Prerequisites:** Chip, Material UI component catalog, Component Libraries: Material UI, Pagination Query Parameters, MUI Supported Components, JSX and Rendering, Dialog, Material UI deep imports for bundle size This chapter is a reference roundup. The headline topic is the bundle-size story for Material UI: why `@mui/material` and `@mui/icons-material` barrel imports are slow on the developer machine, how to enforce deep imports with ESLint, and how to keep your IDE from re-introducing barrel imports through auto-complete. The page then summarises the neighbouring MUI primitives the rest of the roundup covers: `ButtonGroup`, `Card` (and its composition parts), `CircularProgress`, `ClickAwayListener`, `theme.containerQueries`, `CssBaseline` (and `ScopedCssBaseline`), MUI's deprecation lifecycle, dialog and snackbar feedback, the FAQ practices that come up most, `Fab`, and the SVG / `SvgIcon` / `createSvgIcon` icon path. The two exercises at the end combine most of these into one UI slice and then re-type the slice under strict TypeScript.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Material UI's package layout is a directory of files, one default export per file, plus one barrel file (`index.js`) that re-exports them all. Modern bundlers tree-shake the production bundle, so the size on a deployed CDN is the same either way. The cost shows up on the developer machine, where the bundler has to walk every named export of the barrel to learn which symbols exist before it can throw a `ReferenceError` when you mistype one. `@mui/icons-material` is worse than `@mui/material`: it ships 2,100+ icons in the barrel, and the parse takes long enough to watch. Importing each component by its own path side-steps the barrel. The dev server sees the one file you need and skips the rest. ESLint stops the rule from being silently broken, the IDE auto-import exclusion stops VS Code from re-introducing the barrel, and the codemod migrates existing barrel imports in bulk.

Key Code / CLI Example
import Button from '@mui/material/Button';
import DeleteIcon from '@mui/icons-material/Delete';

export default function ConfirmDelete() {
  return (
    <Button
      variant="contained"
      color="error"
      startIcon={<DeleteIcon />}
      onClick={() => console.log('confirmed')}
    >
      Delete account
    </Button>
  );
}
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

ESLint with the `no-restricted-imports` pattern from above reports: Replace with `import Button from '@mui/material/Button';`. Add `@mui/icons-material/[IconName]` for icons. VS Code by default offers `Button` from `@mui/material` first. Add `typescript.preferences.autoImportSpecifierExcludeRegexes` from above, or accept the suggestion, then let ESLint flag it. `@mui/icons-material` depends on `@mui/material`, which depends on Emotion. Installing the icon package without the core produces runtime errors when the first icon mounts:

**Difficulty:** 1-2 · **Prerequisites:** Component Libraries: Material UI, Chip, MUI Avatar, MUI Supported Components, Material UI component catalog, MUI Bundle Size Optimization, Pagination Query Parameters This is a reference roundup built around the icon package that most Material UI screens depend on. The namesake is `@mui/icons-material`, the package that ships the official Material Icons as React components. Around it sits the set of components you reach for in the same breath: the `ImageList` grid, the layout primitives (`Box`, `Stack`, `Grid`), the `LinearProgress` bar, the `List` family, the `Rating` and `SpeedDial` interactive surfaces, the Base-UI-composed `NumberField`, and the two customization APIs (`classes` and `slots` / `slotProps`) that every one of these components exposes. Localization, right-to-left layout, and the documentation MCP server close it out.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

`@mui/icons-material` converts the 2,100+ official Material Icons into `SvgIcon`-based React components. Each icon is a named export, and each name follows a predictable scheme: the icon's Material name in PascalCase, with an optional theme suffix. The five themes are `Filled` (the default, no suffix), `Outlined`, `Rounded`, `TwoTone`, and `Sharp`. An icon whose Material name starts with a digit is prefixed so it stays a valid identifier: the "3D Rotation" icon is `ThreeDRotation`.

Key Code / CLI Example
bun add @mui/material @emotion/react @emotion/styled
bun add @mui/icons-material
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

Direct DOM mutation or impure side effects during the render phase cause hydration mismatches, duplicate executions in Strict Mode, and stale closures. Always declare full dependency arrays in useEffect and never read state during render from outside the component tree.

**Difficulty:** 1-2 · **Prerequisites:** Component Libraries: Material UI, Pagination Query Parameters, Material UI component catalog This chapter is a reference roundup built around the `Stepper` family, the wizard-like workflow surface that comes up in every multi-step form (checkout, onboarding, settings with validation steps, KYC, signup). Around the `Stepper` sits the constellation of MUI parts a stepper naturally composes with: the `SvgIcon` wrapper and the `@mui/icons-material` package that put a check mark on completed steps, the `sx` prop and the wider customization strategy that retunes a step's look, the `Table` family for the "summary" final step in many wizards, `Tabs` for the variant where the steps are peers rather than a sequence, the `TextField` and `NumberField` inputs that fill each step's body, `ToggleButton` for binary choices in a step, nested `ThemeProvider`s to give the wizard its own palette, and the polymorphic `component` prop that swaps the step root for a router link when the wizard drives a URL.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

A `Stepper` is a numbered, sequenced indicator. You feed it the steps (an array of labels) and tell it which one is active; it paints the icons, the connectors, and the labels in the correct state. The pattern is "active / completed / disabled / error" on every step, with a connector rule between each pair. The `Stepper` only paints the indicator. The body of each step lives outside the indicator; you keep a `currentStep` index in your component and render a different `<Box>` (or `StepContent`) based on that index. The component gives you the chrome, you own the body and the navigation.

Key Code / CLI Example
bun add @mui/material @emotion/react @emotion/styled
bun add @mui/icons-material
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

Direct DOM mutation or impure side effects during the render phase cause hydration mismatches, duplicate executions in Strict Mode, and stale closures. Always declare full dependency arrays in useEffect and never read state during render from outside the component tree.

Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 1-2 · **Prerequisites:** Component Libraries: Material UI, Material UI component catalog, Chip This chapter opens the positioning layer of Material UI. `Popper` is the low-level primitive that places any floating content next to an anchor, and three of the most-used composite components (`Tooltip`, `Menu`, `Autocomplete`) are built on top of it. The reference sections after `Popper` cover the rest of the components in the brief: `Box`, `Stack`, `Paper`, `Tabs`, the `@mui/icons-material` package, right-to-left support, root and nested prop forwarding, and the Emotion vs `@mui/styled-engine-sc` choice. Each section is what the component is for, the props you reach for, and one minimal JSX. The two exercises at the end build a real `Autocomplete` and a Tabs-driven settings panel.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

A `Popper` is a positioning engine, not a UI element. You give it an `anchorEl` (the thing you want to float content next to) and a child, and the child lands where the browser viewport and Popper's placement logic say it should land. The component itself draws no border, no background, and no shadow. It is the anchor + the child + the math that connects them. 1. `Popper` renders into a `Portal` at `document.body` by default. The floating content escapes any `overflow: hidden` or `transform: 3d` ancestor on the trigger. This is why tooltips survive inside scrolling drawers. 2. `Popper` does not block scrolling, does not close on click-away, and does not manage focus. Those are jobs for `Popover` and `Dialog`, which wrap `Popper` and add the modal behaviour.

Key Code / CLI Example
import { useRef, useState } from "react";
import Popper from "@mui/material/Popper";
import Box from "@mui/material/Box";

export default function HoverHint() {
  const [anchor, setAnchor] = useState<HTMLElement | null>(null);
  return (
    <>
      <button
        ref={useRef(null)}
        onMouseEnter={(event) => {
          setAnchor(event.currentTarget);
        }}
        onMouseLeave={() => {
          setAnchor(null);
        }}
      >
        Hover me
      </button>

Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 1-2 · **Prerequisites:** Component Libraries: Material UI, Material UI component catalog, Chip This chapter opens the positioning layer of Material UI. `Popper` is the low-level primitive that places any floating content next to an anchor, and three of the most-used composite components (`Tooltip`, `Menu`, `Autocomplete`) are built on top of it. The reference sections after `Popper` cover the rest of the components in the brief: `Box`, `Stack`, `Paper`, `Tabs`, the `@mui/icons-material` package, right-to-left support, root and nested prop forwarding, and the Emotion vs `@mui/styled-engine-sc` choice. Each section is what the component is for, the props you reach for, and one minimal JSX. The two exercises at the end build a real `Autocomplete` and a Tabs-driven settings panel.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

A `Popper` is a positioning engine, not a UI element. You give it an `anchorEl` (the thing you want to float content next to) and a child, and the child lands where the browser viewport and Popper's placement logic say it should land. The component itself draws no border, no background, and no shadow. It is the anchor + the child + the math that connects them. 1. `Popper` renders into a `Portal` at `document.body` by default. The floating content escapes any `overflow: hidden` or `transform: 3d` ancestor on the trigger. This is why tooltips survive inside scrolling drawers. 2. `Popper` does not block scrolling, does not close on click-away, and does not manage focus. Those are jobs for `Popover` and `Dialog`, which wrap `Popper` and add the modal behaviour.

Key Code / CLI Example
import { useRef, useState } from "react";
import Popper from "@mui/material/Popper";
import Box from "@mui/material/Box";

export default function HoverHint() {
  const [anchor, setAnchor] = useState<HTMLElement | null>(null);
  return (
    <>
      <button
        ref={useRef(null)}
        onMouseEnter={(event) => {
          setAnchor(event.currentTarget);
        }}
        onMouseLeave={() => {
          setAnchor(null);
        }}
      >
        Hover me
      </button>
      <Popper open={Boolean(anchor)} anchorEl={anchor} placement="top">
        <Box sx={{ p: 1, bgcolor: "background.paper", boxShadow: 3 }}>
          Floating hint
        </Box>
      </Popper>
    </>
  );
}

If you call `setAnchor(null)` to close, the popper unmounts. If you keep `anchorEl` set and just flip `open` to `false`, the popper unmounts as well, but the next render starts with no target to measure against, which produces a one-frame flash if you re-mount quickly. Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 1-2 · **Prerequisites:** Component Libraries: Material UI, Material UI component catalog, Material UI Color System, Dialog, Popper This chapter is a reference roundup built around the `Timeline` component, the chronological list surface that comes up in changelogs, order histories, audit logs, and activity feeds. Around the `Timeline` sits the larger MUI layout and theming toolkit a `Timeline` composes with: the `theme.breakpoints` API (the five screen-width keys and the `up` / `down` / `only` / `between` helpers) that lets the layout collapse from alternating to single-column on small screens, `Container` for horizontally centered page content, `Grid` (MUI 6 layout grid) for the responsive two-column variant of the `Timeline`, the `theme.components` overrides system that tunes every `TimelineDot` in the app at once, density props that tighten the `Timeline` on dense surfaces, `defaultProps` merging for class-name and style defaults, routing integration for the optional click-through timeline, palette tokens for the dot colour, `theme.spacing()` for the row gap, and `Stack` for the inner content column.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

A `Timeline` is a chronological list. Each entry is a `TimelineItem` whose visual structure is a `TimelineSeparator` (the line and the dot) sitting next to a `TimelineContent` (the title and body). The optional `TimelineOppositeContent` provides a second column used for dates or timestamps in alternating layouts. The `Timeline` owns chrome (lines, dots, spacing). The `TimelineContent` is yours to fill: a typography node, a card, a button, a `Stack` of chips. The component is open enough to render anything inside the content slot but opinionated enough to keep the visual rhythm consistent.

Key Code / CLI Example
bun add @mui/material @emotion/react @emotion/styled
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

Direct DOM mutation or impure side effects during the render phase cause hydration mismatches, duplicate executions in Strict Mode, and stale closures. Always declare full dependency arrays in useEffect and never read state during render from outside the component tree.

Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 1-3 · **Prerequisites:** Component Libraries: Material UI, Chip, Material UI component catalog, MUI Timeline component, Popper This chapter opens with the Grid v2 migration, which renames the legacy grid (`@mui/material/Grid` in v6, `@mui/material/GridLegacy` in v7) and lands the new layout grid at `@mui/material/Grid` (v7) or `@mui/material/Grid2` (v6), with collapsed `size={{ xs, sm, md, ... }}` props and a removed `item` prop. Around the migration sits the rest of the MUI vocabulary the new grid composes with: `theme.typography` and the `Typography` and `Link` components that style every text node, the `Typography` `variantMapping` that decouples visual variant from semantic HTML, `responsiveFontSizes()` for media-query-driven type scales, the `theme.transitions.create()` and `getAutoHeightDuration()` helpers plus `theme.motion.reducedMotion` that keep motion consistent across the UI, `ImageList` (and its quilted / woven / masonry variants) for repeated image grids, `Tooltip` for accessible labels on hover / focus / long-press, and the `unstable_ClassNameGenerator` build-time hook that rewrites every MUI component class prefix across the app before any `@mui/*` import is evaluated.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

The new layout grid (Grid v2, also called the modern Grid) is the same flexbox idea as before: a `container` with `size`-driven children that break onto multiple lines at the theme breakpoints. What changed is the API surface. Per-breakpoint props collapsed into a single `size` object, the `item` flag disappeared, the `offset` feature replaced `zeroMinWidth`, and the grid now uses CSS variables instead of nested negative margins (so it no longer overflows the container). The migration is a one-time rewrite of an import path and a few prop names, with a codemod that does most of the rename for you. subgraph v6 [MUI v6] V6Import["import Grid from '@mui/material/Grid2'"] V6Props["size={{ xs: 12, sm: 6 }}"] V6Import --> V6Grid["Modern Grid (Grid2 import)"] V6Props --> V6Grid end

Key Code / CLI Example
bun add @mui/material @emotion/react @emotion/styled
bun add @mui/icons-material
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

The codemod is keyed on the import path. Run it after the rename or it skips the file. Either un-wrap the inner `<Grid>` (rename one of them), or do the prop rename by hand. The codemod's source-matcher only catches direct `<Grid>` JSX. Missing weights fall back to browser synthetic bold / light, which never matches real Roboto. The MUI docs flag the four weights explicitly. `hyphens-auto` is language-aware and depends on a `lang` attribute somewhere up the tree (the standard place is on `<html>` or the section root). A `<Typography lang="en">` works for that node, but if you put `lang` only on the `Typography` and not on the surrounding `ImageList` or `Box`, the rest of the tree still uses the document language.

Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 3 · **Prerequisites:** Material UI component catalog, MUI Timeline component, Chip, Dialog, Material UI MCP documentation server, Tailwind theme variables This chapter opens with the `createTheme(options)` rule that catches people the first time they try to derive one theme option from another: build the base theme first, then derive the dependent values from it. Around that rule sits the rest of the MUI architecture vocabulary a real application leans on: `theme.containerQueries` (and the `@<size>` `sx` shorthand) for sizing against the parent container rather than the viewport, the `styled` / `ownerState` / `useThemeProps` pattern for building components that participate in the theme, `enhanceHighContrast` for Windows High Contrast Mode support, `Autocomplete` for searchable selects with separately tracked input text and selected value, CSS cascade layers (`enableCssLayer: true` plus a named `mui` layer or modular sublayers) for ordering framework and application styles, the `@material-ui/pickers` to `@mui/x-date-pickers` migration (with `Desktop*` / `Mobile*` / `Static*` exports and `LocalizationProvider`), right-to-left support (`dir` attribute, `theme.direction: 'rtl'`, RTL Stylis plugin), the Tailwind v4 CSS layers integration (`@layer mui` plus `@layer utilities` plus `@theme inline`), and the v4 → v5 → v6 → v7 → v9 upgrade ladder (codemods, Emotion peer deps, Grid rename, ESM-only, slots/slotProps, system-props codemod).

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

`createTheme(options)` is a normalising pass: it merges your `options` over the default theme, computes derived values (palette light/dark variants, typography rem sizes, breakpoint helpers), and returns the resolved theme. A dependent option is one whose value must read from another resolved option. The dependency has to be resolved at construction time, not at module load time, so the practical shape is "build the base theme in one call, derive the dependent options from it in a second call". The same shape applies when you receive a theme as a prop (for instance from a `ThemeProvider` parent) and want to extend it: read the prop, derive the dependent values, return a new theme object. Forward-compatibility matters: an independently supplied options object should be merged into the *first* argument of the next `createTheme`, so the call is `(input, ...rest) => createTheme(deepmerge(base, input), ...rest)` rather than two separate calls.

Key Code / CLI Example
bun add @mui/material @emotion/react @emotion/styled
bun add @mui/icons-material
bun add @mui/lab
bun add @mui/x-date-pickers
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

`createTheme` is the normalising pass. Reading from raw options gives you the literal you wrote in, not the resolved value. The base theme is what you should read from. The first argument is the resolved theme to extend; the second is the new options. Independent options objects should be merged into the first argument rather than chained through separate calls. <Grid container> <Grid2 size={6}>A</Grid2> </Grid> ``` <Grid container> <Grid size={6}>A</Grid> </Grid> ```

**Difficulty:** 2-3 · **Prerequisites:** Component Libraries: Material UI, Chip, Material UI component catalog, Material UI theme provider, MUI Timeline component This chapter opens with the integration that lets Material UI and Tailwind v4 share the same DOM without `!important` wars: CSS cascade layers. MUI ships `experimental_extendTheme({ cssLayers: { ... } })` (and the corresponding `enableCssLayer` on the theme) to wrap every generated Emotion stylesheet in `@layer mui.global`, `@layer mui.components`, `@layer mui.theme`, `@layer mui.custom`, and `@layer mui.sx`; Tailwind v4 reads those layers and orders its own utilities last, so a `className="bg-red-500"` always wins. Around the integration sits the rest of the MUI vocabulary the layered theme composes with: the documented `Menubar` recipe that composes Base UI's primitives with MUI components, the `NumberField` recipe that wires Base UI's `NumberField` to MUI form controls, the JSS to Emotion migration path for v4 to v5 codebases, the MUI API design conventions (low-level composition, consistent prop naming, root prop spreading, slot customisation, controlled state, root ref forwarding), the `Autocomplete` combobox (props like `options`, `value`/`onChange`, `inputValue`/`onInputChange`, `getOptionLabel`, `isOptionEqualToValue`, `multiple`, `freeSolo`, `groupBy`, `renderGroup`, `renderInput`, `renderOption`, `filterOptions`, `createFilterOptions`, plus the headless `useAutocomplete`), the v9 upgrade highlights (Enter/Space clicks now bubble as `MouseEvent`, the `nativeButton` prop for `<div>`-based custom buttons, the `AutocompleteValueOrFreeSoloValueMapping` typing for `freeSolo`, `Backdrop` no longer adding `aria-hidden` by default), the `unstable_ClassNameGenerator` build-time hook for rewriting the MUI class-name prefix, the composition guide (forwarded props, `muiName` preservation, 🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

CSS cascade layers (`@layer a, b, c;`) define a strict order of precedence across the whole stylesheet. A rule inside `@layer a` always loses to a rule in `@layer b`, regardless of selector specificity. Tailwind v4 emits every utility class inside `@layer utilities;` so that any user-land `@layer theme` or `@layer components` overrides are guaranteed to lose to a Tailwind utility. The MUI integration simply wraps every Emotion-generated stylesheet inside `@layer mui.*` so it sits inside the cascade order too. With both sides agreeing on the layer order, you never need `!important`. L1["@layer theme, base"]:::base L2["@layer mui.global"]:::mui L3["@layer mui.components"]:::mui L4["@layer mui.theme"]:::mui L5["@layer mui.custom"]:::mui L6["@layer mui.sx"]:::mui L7["@layer components"]:::base L8["@layer utilities"]:::tw

Key Code / CLI Example
bun add @mui/material @emotion/react @emotion/styled

Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 2-3 · **Prerequisites:** Component Libraries: Material UI, Material UI component catalog, Dialog, Popper, MUI Timeline component This chapter is a reference roundup built around the `Masonry` component, the variable-height, Pinterest-style column layout. Around `Masonry` sits the wider overlay ecosystem a `Masonry` host page usually pairs with: `Modal` (the foundation that `Dialog`, `Drawer`, `Menu`, and `Popover` all build on), `Drawer` for side navigation, `Popover` for anchored floating content, `Menu` and `Popper` for menus and tooltips, `Menubar` for top-level menus composed on top of Base UI's primitive, `Native Color` for opting the theme into CSS `color-mix()` and relative-color syntax, `Pigment CSS` for zero-runtime CSS-in-JS, and the styled-engine choice between Emotion and `@mui/styled-engine-sc`.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

A `Masonry` packs variable-height blocks at a uniform width into N columns. Each new block goes into the shortest column, which avoids the "ragged bottom" you get with CSS grid when row heights differ. The component is not a CSS grid; it is a JS layout that measures every block and places it manually, which is what makes the no-vertical-gap packing possible. Three details that drive every `Masonry` you write:

Key Code / CLI Example
bun add @mui/material @emotion/react @emotion/styled
bun add @mui/icons-material
bun add @mui/lab   # optional: Lab ships Masonry in some MUI versions
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

`Masonry` measures and places each child in JavaScript. Wrapping the container in `display: grid` interferes with the column math. Use `Masonry`'s own column/spacing props, or use `Grid` (MUI 6 layout grid) when you want CSS grid behaviour. Without it, the server renders an empty placeholder under each column and the page jumps on hydration. Set `defaultHeight` (and `defaultColumns`, `defaultSpacing`) to match the post-hydration layout. `Modal` is the foundation; it does not bring visuals. Reach for the composite component that matches the user intent. Use `Modal` only when the surface is custom (a centred Card with bespoke padding and transitions). `Popper` does not close on outside click. If you want a dropdown that dismisses itself, use `Popover` (or `Menu`). `Popper` is the right pr

Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Prerequisites:** MUI Supported Components, Material UI component catalog, Material UI Color System, Popper, MUI Timeline component, Material UI Grid v2 migration This chapter is a reference-heavy lesson. Its main subject is composing MUI's table parts into a usable data surface. The later sections collect related MUI API and migration patterns that often appear beside a table in a real application.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

You meet this composition pattern in invoices, audit logs, product lists, and admin screens. It prevents three different bug classes: invalid table markup that confuses assistive technology, unstable row identity that makes reconciliation reuse the wrong DOM, and controls whose labels change while the displayed data stays unchanged. Use a plain composed `Table` when you need a table-shaped view and you want control over markup. Move to MUI `DataGrid` when the feature set grows into a large data-management surface with virtualization, column menus, richer filtering, editing, or server-side models. `DataGrid` is a separate product with a different API. It is not a drop-in replacement for the composition tree above.

Key Code / CLI Example
import Table from "@mui/material/Table";
import TableBody from "@mui/material/TableBody";
import TableCell from "@mui/material/TableCell";
import TableHead from "@mui/material/TableHead";
import TableRow from "@mui/material/TableRow";

export function SmallTable() {
  return (
    <Table aria-label="two products">
      <TableHead>
        <TableRow>
          <TableCell component="th" scope="col">
            Product
          </TableCell>
          <TableCell component="th" scope="col" align="right">
            Stock
          </TableCell>
        </TableRow>
      </TableHead>
      <TableBody>
        <TableRow key="pen">
          <TableCell component="th" scope="row">
            Pen
          </TableCell>
          <TableCell align="right">18</TableCell>
        </TableRow>
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

This compiles, but sorting causes React to reuse the wrong row instance when a row contains local state or an input. React may log: That warning appears when there is no key. Using `key={index}` silences it but still gives rows identities tied to their current positions. Use `key={row.id}` with an ID that does not change when the order changes. This broken TypeScript is intentional: With MUI's `TableCellProps`, TypeScript reports:

Expand NotesCollapse
Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 3 · **Prerequisites:** MUI Table Composition, Component Libraries: Material UI, useActionState + React 19 Form Actions, MUI Masonry, Material UI theme provider

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

A shared brand package can serve several products while each product chooses its palette, navigation, and component behavior. Explicit merging makes that boundary visible in code. Ordered style arrays prevent a release from silently removing focus, hover, or disabled-state rules. Avoiding an eager deep merge also keeps theme construction out of the render path and removes avoidable startup work. The component roundup gives the merged theme real consumers: a `Drawer` or `Menu` for navigation, a `Dialog` or `Backdrop` for attention, and controlled input components for preferences. Each consumer reads the final theme from `ThemeProvider`, so a change to brand tokens reaches the whole tree without prop drilling.

Key Code / CLI Example
import { createTheme } from '@mui/material/styles';
import type { ThemeOptions } from '@mui/material/styles';

const brand: ThemeOptions = {
  palette: { primary: { main: '#111827' } },
  shape: { borderRadius: 6 },
};

const appTheme = createTheme({
  ...brand,
  palette: {
    ...brand.palette,
    primary: { ...brand.palette?.primary, main: '#2563eb' },
  },
});
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

The code compiles, but the brand's `minWidth` and pseudo-class rules vanish. Spread the branded `MuiButton` entry and put the two roots in an array. Spread `brand.palette.primary` before changing `main`, and repeat that pattern for nested groups you customize. If you render `<Switch checked={enabled} />` without an `onChange` that updates `enabled`, the control looks stuck. React does not change the prop for you. Keep the source of truth in state. `ToggleButtonGroup` calls its handler with `null` after the selected button is clicked again. Passing that value into a state typed as `View` produces `Type 'null' is not assignable to type 'View'`. Check `next !== null` before updating.

**Prerequisites:** useActionState + React 19 Form Actions, useContext, Forms with React Hook Form, Component Libraries: Material UI, Material UI component catalog, MUI Table Composition, MUI Timeline component, Material UI MCP documentation server, Chip This is a reference-heavy chapter. It starts with tabs, then collects MUI form controls and styling APIs that use the same two ideas: controlled values and context shared by a parent component.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

You meet these components in settings screens, onboarding flows, search filters, review forms, and admin tools. A shared controlled-value model makes their behavior predictable, while the MUI parent handles focus and keyboard details that are easy to omit in hand-built widgets. The context hooks and slot APIs also create supported customization boundaries. They prevent code from reaching into private markup or copying internal state. Migration work then becomes a change of package, styling engine, or extraction model without rewriting the form's domain state.

Key Code / CLI Example
import { useState } from "react";
import type { SyntheticEvent } from "react";
import Tab from "@mui/material/Tab";
import Tabs from "@mui/material/Tabs";

export function AccountTabs() {
  const [active, setActive] = useState<"profile" | "security">("profile");

  const selectTab = (_event: SyntheticEvent, next: string): void => {
    if (next === "profile" || next === "security") {
      setActive(next);
    }
  };

  return (
    <section>
      <Tabs value={active} onChange={selectTab} aria-label="Account sections">
        <Tab
          value="profile"
          label="Profile"
          id="account-tab-profile"
          aria-controls="account-panel-profile"
        />
        <Tab
          value="security"
          label="Security"
          id="account-tab-security"
          ar
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

A `Tab` with `aria-controls="security-panel"` and a panel with `id="profile-panel"` compiles and does not log a runtime error. The accessibility tree loses the relationship. Derive both IDs from the same tab value, or use the Lab components to wire the relationship. This deliberately broken TypeScript drops the clear state: Use `useState<number | null>(3)` or reject `null` deliberately when the product requires a rating. An `Autocomplete` value loaded from one request may have the same fields as an option loaded from another request, but it is a different object reference.
