Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 1-4 · **Prerequisites:** Chip, Material UI Color System, MUI Table Composition, Components and Props, Domain-first data model planning, React Canary Release Channel This chapter opens with **Pigment CSS**, MUI's zero-runtime CSS-in-JS engine: it pre-compiles styles at build time, emits real CSS, and is the path forward if you want a `styled`-like authoring experience while staying React Server Components compatible. Around that headline sits the rest of the styling vocabulary that the longer Styling section has been pulling together. The Pigment CSS APIs (`css`, `globalCss`, `keyframes`, `styled`, `variants`, runtime callbacks) are covered in depth, the Vite and Next.js plugins are explained as the entry points, the `extendTheme` / `vars` pattern is shown as the bridge between the build-time theme and runtime CSS variables, and the `sx` prop is described as the inline-style escape hatch that compiles down to `className` + `style` at build time. The roundup that follows covers the older Material UI `TypographyProps`-based polymorphic wrapper pattern, the v7 and v9 upgrade steps (package exports, slot standardisation, CSS layers, Grid renaming, accessibility improvements), the two halves of `prettier-plugin-tailwindcss` (fixed-order sorting and the v1.7+ collapse pass for whitespace and duplicates), the early `@tailwindui/react` `<Transition>` primitive, the shadcn UI copy-paste model that re-shapes how a team owns its component library, CSS Modules as a third styling option next to Pigment and Tailwind, the Wieruch component-tree / `createRoot` / one-way data flow foundations, and the extraction heuristic that keeps a component understandable.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

A "CSS-in-JS" library writes a stylesheet that ships JavaScript to the browser, then inserts rules into the DOM on render. Emotion (the engine behind `@mui/material`) does this. The runtime cost is real: every render has to diff the styles, and the styles themselves have to live in the bundle. Pigment CSS inverts the relationship. The `css` and `styled` calls are still TypeScript, but a build plugin (Vite or Next.js) reads the source, emits a real CSS file, and rewrites the call sites so the runtime only does `className` lookup. The browser sees a `<link rel="stylesheet">` and a class string, nothing more. The build-time flavour has three consequences worth naming up front:

Key Code / CLI Example
bun add @mui/material @emotion/react @emotion/styled
bun add @pigment-css/react
bun add --save-dev @pigment-css/vite-plugin
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

**1. Forgetting the stylesheet import.** The Pigment CSS build plugin writes the CSS file, but the bundler does not know to serve it. The browser shows a flash of unstyled content followed by the layout, because the CSS is loaded but its `<link>` is in the wrong place. Fix: createRoot(document.getElementById("root")!).render(<App />); ``` **2. Using `useTheme` from `@mui/material/styles` instead of `@mui/material-pigment-css`.** The first is the Emotion runtime hook and returns the resolved theme object; the second is the Pigment CSS hook and returns the `theme.vars` proxy. The types are similar but the values differ. The Emotion hook works in Pigment projects only because the Emotion engine is still installed; the values are the resolved objects, not the CSS variables. The Pigment hook

Core Definition & Architectural Role

**Difficulty:** 2-3 · **Prerequisites:** JSX and Rendering, Components and Props, preconnect, Chip, React Major Version Policy, Vite modern web constraints, React Canary Release Channel This chapter opens with the **Shadcn UI + Base UI + Tailwind component library** model: you don't `npm install` a styled component library anymore, you run an init command, the CLI copies the source for each primitive into `src/components/ui/`, and you own the result. Around that headline sits the rest of the styling vocabulary the Styling section has been collecting: `class-variance-authority` (`cva`) for typed variant strings, `tailwind-merge` to dedupe conflicting utilities, Base UI as the headless accessibility layer underneath, the Tailwind UI Spotlight personal-site template as the canonical "put it all together" example, stable keys for list identity in the project list, the styled-components library as the alternative CSS-in-JS authoring style (tagged-template literals, `.attrs()` for non-class props, extending via `styled(BaseComponent)`), the `babel-plugin-styled-components` companion that makes DevTools class names readable, the Pocket template's Framer Motion entrance animations, the Thinking-in-React decomposition heuristic, Vite CSS Modules as the third styling option (alongside Tailwind and CSS-in-JS), the framework-agnostic `@tailwindplus/elements` custom-element library, and the Wieruch component-tree / `createRoot` / one-way data flow foundations that hold the whole stack together.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

A traditional component library ships as a black-box npm package. You import `Button` from `@mui/material`, you call `<Button>`, and the source for `Button` lives somewhere in `node_modules`. Customising it means either (a) wrapping it in your own component that overrides `sx` or `className` props, or (b) forking the package and shipping a private build. The Shadcn UI model inverts the relationship. Instead of a black box, you get a folder of small files you wrote (or the CLI wrote for you), styled with `cva` variants, layered on top of unstyled accessibility primitives from Base UI, and rendered with Tailwind utility classes. The "library" lives in your repo. The dependency on `@base-ui-components/react` is the only third-party surface; everything else is your own source.

Key Code / CLI Example
// src/components/ui/card.tsx
import { forwardRef, type HTMLAttributes } from "react";
import { cn } from "@/lib/utils";

export const Card = forwardRef<HTMLDivElement, HTMLAttributes<HTMLDivElement>>(
  ({ className, ...props }, ref) => (
    <div
      ref={ref}
      className={cn(
        "rounded-lg border bg-card text-card-foreground shadow-sm",
        className,
      )}
      {...props}
    />
  ),
);
Card.displayName = "Card";
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

If a caller passes `className="bg-red-500"`, the rendered class is `"... bg-primary ... bg-red-500"`. The browser applies the **last** declaration in the stylesheet, not the last class in the string. With Tailwind, all utility classes live in the same generated layer at the same specificity, so the order in the class string *does* matter, but only when Tailwind's ordering rules are followed. For un-common pairs, you get the wrong winner, or you get both utilities emitted and the visual is whichever class the JIT put later in the sheet. `twMerge` removes the ambiguity by parsing the utilities and dropping the conflicting earlier one. `cva` returns a *function* from a config. If the config object is recreated on every render, the returned function is a new identity on every render. Any cons

📝Comprehensive Study Notes & Mental ModelQuick Review
Expand NotesCollapse
Core Definition & Architectural Role

A styled-component is a React component whose styles live in a tagged template literal right next to the component. You write CSS in the template, and the library returns a real component you render like any other: const Button = styled.button` padding: 8px 16px; border-radius: 6px; border: none; background: #0a84ff; color: white; `;

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

A themed component library is two systems working together. The theme plus typed templates give you styles that read from one design source and cannot silently misspell a token. The state architecture (minimal state, a clear owner, lifting, and the controlled-versus- uncontrolled choice) decides what those styles react to and keeps the values that drive them in exactly one place. Get the theme typed and the ownership right, and a tab strip, a paginator, a stepper, and a form all end up with the same predictable shape: value down, change up, styles derived from the theme.

Key Code / CLI Example
import styled from "styled-components";

const Button = styled.button`
  padding: 8px 16px;
  border-radius: 6px;
  border: none;
  background: #0a84ff;
  color: white;
`;

// <Button>Save</Button>  ->  a <button> with those styles attached
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

Without `ThemeProps<AppTheme>` (or a `DefaultTheme` augmentation), `props.theme` widens to `any` and `colours` (British misspelling) sails through the compiler. Type the theme once and the typo becomes an error at the call site. Rename it `$filled`. The transient prefix keeps the prop out of the rendered attributes while still feeding the interpolation. Keeping a `filteredList` in `useState` and updating it in an effect gives you two sources of truth that drift. Compute the filtered list from the source list and the query during render. State holds only the inputs; the output is derived. If two siblings each keep their own copy of the "same" value, they will disagree the moment one updates without the other. Lift the value into their common parent and pass it down. One owner, one value.
